profiles.meeting_scenario: A university visualization lab and a municipal stormwater operations department are planning a 10-week pilot project inspired by design by immersion. The goal is to let the visualization researcher learn operational pain points by participating in parts of the city's spring storm-response workflow, then use those insights to shape a visualization concept that is useful to the city and potentially informative for a future methodological publication on transdisciplinary collaboration. The meeting is a planning session to align on how the immersion will happen, what preparation is needed, which April workshop will anchor the timeline, what documentation will be produced, and who owns each step. The expected outcome is a shared plan for the immersion schedule, participant involvement, workshop preparation, and post-immersion deliverables.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.role: Associate Professor of Visualization and Pilot Project Lead
members.expertise: Problem-driven visualization, qualitative field methods, design studies, interdisciplinary research
members.background: Lena runs a university visualization lab that collaborates with public-sector partners on operational analytics tools; she has published design studies and is building a new line of work around design by immersion.
members.private_state: She wants this pilot to produce enough real-world engagement to justify a future grant and paper, but she also needs to fit the work around teaching and cannot spend full operational shifts in the field.
hidden_assumptions: An 'immersion week' in design research usually means sampling the most informative moments across a period, not being physically embedded for every shift.
When someone says 'the April workshop,' they are probably referring to the co-design session already blocked on the university calendar with sticky notes, sketches, and discussion prompts.
Routine collaboration documentation can include de-identified field notes, photos of work settings, and reflective process memos unless a partner explicitly restricts them.
Operational access for observation will mostly happen during weekday daytime hours unless someone specifically mentions emergency or overnight coverage.

members.name: Marcus Hale
members.expertise: Municipal field operations, emergency coordination, crew scheduling, infrastructure maintenance
members.background: Marcus oversees dispatch, field crews, and seasonal preparedness for the city's stormwater division; he has worked with vendors and consultants before but not with academic visualization researchers.
members.private_state: He wants the collaboration to yield something practical for his team before peak rain season, while minimizing burden on staff and avoiding any public exposure of internal operations without formal clearance.
hidden_assumptions: If an outside collaborator says they want to be 'immersed' or 'shadow operations,' that means joining the team through full shifts, including off-hours activity where real issues appear.
Around his department, 'the April workshop' naturally refers to the annual resilience tabletop exercise, because that is the only April workshop staff seriously prepare for.
Municipal operational photos, room layouts, and raw field notes are internal by default even in collaborative projects, unless communications or legal explicitly approves release.
Once he sponsors a visitor, safety gear and access logistics are routine administrative details rather than planning items that need discussion.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as an immersion week
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about Lena being 'embedded' or doing an 'immersion week' with operations.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means selective participation in key activities across roughly two weeks: morning briefings, a few ride-alongs, and follow-up conversations totaling around 15-20 hours.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means one continuous week of full-shift shadowing, including after-hours callouts if weather triggers them.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see immersion as obviously valuable and use the same research-friendly language, but neither thinks to convert it into hours, shifts, or exact attendance because the term feels self-explanatory and flexible.

misalignment_points.topic: Which April workshop anchors the plan
misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly say they want the prototype and staff ready 'for the April workshop.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the university-hosted co-design workshop on April 18 with paper sketches, discussion prompts, and a small mixed group of researchers and city staff.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the city's annual resilience tabletop exercise on April 24, where staff walk through a storm scenario using operational materials.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both know there is an important workshop in April and the shorthand sounds natural; because each has only one salient workshop on their own calendar, the phrase creates false consensus without prompting date confirmation.

misalignment_points.topic: What the case study documentation includes
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to produce a 'case study package' or 'documentation' after immersion.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the package includes de-identified observation notes, photos of the dispatch room and field context, a reflective memo about the collaboration process, and material that can later support a paper or grant appendix.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the package means an internal summary for the department: workflow observations, practical recommendations, and perhaps annotated screenshots, but no reusable publication-oriented material or operational imagery beyond internal circulation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Documentation sounds like a mundane wrap-up task rather than a substantive design decision, so each person silently fills in the scope using their institution's normal practice and hears the other's wording as compatible.

turns.inner_thought: I need a workable plan that gives me enough contact with their real setting to ground a prototype and eventually support a grant story, but I cannot disappear into operations for days at a time. If we work backward from the April workshop on the university calendar, I can use that co-design session as the forcing function for synthesis and sketching.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time, Marcus. I was hoping today we could map out the immersion plan and then work backward from the April workshop so the pilot stays on schedule.

turns.inner_thought: That timing works. If she's going to be immersed, it really needs to happen as a proper week with the team before everyone gets pulled into prep for the April workshop, meaning the resilience exercise. That's when staff attention gets fragmented, and if weather pops up, she should see what the work actually looks like.
turns.utterance: That makes sense to me. It would help if you can be pretty embedded with the operations team during immersion week, before everyone shifts into prep for the April workshop.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we're aligned on immersion. For me that means sampling the highest-value moments: morning dispatch, a couple ride-alongs, maybe sit with the analysts, spread across the first two weeks of April so I can fit this around teaching and still get a rich enough read on the workflow.
turns.utterance: Yes, absolutely. I was thinking I could join the morning dispatch briefings, ride along with a couple of crews, and spend some time with the analysts across the first two weeks of April.

turns.inner_thought: Those are the right entry points, though the real lessons usually come once the day goes sideways. If she's embedded for the week, she'll catch that anyway, especially if crews are out late or we get a weather-driven callout. No need to belabor it; she seems on board with immersion.
turns.utterance: Those touchpoints should be useful. I will say, some of the most revealing moments tend to happen when crews are still out late or when something weather-driven comes in unexpectedly.

turns.inner_thought: After I synthesize the observation material, I can put together a lightweight prototype and the usual case study package: de-identified notes, some contextual imagery, and a reflective memo. That should give us something concrete to discuss at the April workshop and help me preserve the process for future writing.
turns.utterance: That helps. After the immersion, I can pull together a lightweight prototype and a case study package so we have something concrete for the April workshop.

turns.inner_thought: Good. The department will want a practical packet they can circulate internally after this, not a bunch of raw material floating around. If anything from the control room ends up in the documentation, it should be useful to the team once it's in a clean packet.
turns.utterance: The documentation will be helpful for the department. Anything from the control room is usually most useful once it's in the packet for the team.

turns.inner_thought: That's consistent with normal collaboration documentation. I'll capture field notes, a few photos of the work setting, and a short reflection memo while keeping names out of it. I also need the right mix of people for the April workshop on campus so the discussion is grounded and generative.
turns.utterance: Great. I'll capture field notes, a few contextual photos, and a short reflection memo, and maybe you can identify which staff should participate in the workshop discussion.

turns.inner_thought: For the April workshop, I should bring people who can work through the storm scenario the way they normally would in the tabletop exercise. Dispatch and the analysts are the right mix. If they react using their usual procedures, we'll know whether the prototype is actually useful.
turns.utterance: Yes, I can do that. I'll bring the dispatch supervisor and two analysts to the April workshop so they can react to the scenario using their normal response procedures.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. So the sequence is selective immersion in early April, then a short synthesis window, then the co-design session, then I assemble the case study package for the collaboration record and future reference. This should be enough engagement to show traction without overcommitting my time.
turns.utterance: Okay, so the sequence I'm hearing is: immersion in early April, a short synthesis step, then the workshop, followed by the case study package for the collaboration record.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds settled. I'll make sure badges and safety gear are lined up so she can be with the crew for the week, and then after the April workshop we can review the documentation and decide what the team wants to use internally before rain season ramps up.
turns.utterance: That works for me. I'll handle badges and gear so you can be with the crew for the week, and then we can review the documentation after the workshop.
